text: Inside a traveling-wave tube: how a microwave signal surfs on a beam of electrons.
A traveling-wave tube is a microwave amplifier. Radar, satellite links, electronic warfare — where solid-state amplifiers run out of power.
Everything starts with a hot cathode boiling off electrons.
Twenty thousand volts push them to roughly a quarter of the speed of light.
Left alone the beam destroys itself — like charges repel.
Electrons that hit the helix turn it into a heater. The tube dies.
So a stack of permanent magnets squeezes it back into a pencil about a millimetre wide.
A radio wave travels at the speed of light — far too fast to keep pace with the electrons.
Wound into a helix, the signal must cover about four times more wire than the distance it moves forward. Its forward speed collapses to roughly a quarter of c — exactly the speed of the electrons.
Now the wave and the beam drift along together, and they start to feel each other.
The wave's own electric field sorts the beam: some electrons are slowed, some sped up.
Within a few centimetres the smooth stream has turned into a train of bunches.
The beam is set a hair faster than the wave, so the bunches drift into the region that holds them back — and every electron that is slowed hands its energy straight to the wave.
The signal grows exponentially along the tube.
All of it rests on one thing: the beam the gun actually delivers. Cathode voltage, electrode angles, magnetic field — each one bends the trajectory.
And that trajectory is exactly what this project set out to predict.
